record.paper_title: Multi-D magnetohydrodynamic modelling of pulsar wind nebulae: recent progress and open questions
record.original_question: For pulsar wind nebulae such as the Crab Nebula, how is the pulsar-wind magnetization σ, the ratio of Poynting flux to particle kinetic-energy flux, reduced or redistributed between the highly magnetized light-cylinder region and the wind termination shock, where efficient deceleration requires much lower magnetization, and can three-dimensional high-σ MHD evolution produce a final nebular magnetic field and non-thermal emission consistent with observations?

evidence.quote: According to theoretical models of pulsar magnetospheres, the wind is expected to be highly magnetized near the pulsar light cylinder, where clearly σ ≫ 1. On the other hand, the very first attempts at modelling the Crab nebula within the framework of ideal MHD, showed that effective deceleration of the flow at the TS is only possible if its magnetization is not too high.
However, even in the framework of 2D MHD, the estimated values of σ at the TS are still much smaller than unity, leaving the problem of efficient magnetic dissipation along the way to the shock.

In particular, it is not clear yet whether the average nebular magnetic field strength will be close to that inferred from observations (∼ 200 µG) at the final stage of the evolution, and if the synthetic non-thermal emission will match observational data in all spectral bands, thus confirming the model assumptions on the pulsar wind and emitting particles properties.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a pulsar embedded in a supernova remnant that drives a relativistic magnetized wind into a surrounding nebula (a pulsar wind nebula). Define the wind magnetization parameter σ as the ratio of the Poynting flux to the particle kinetic-energy flux carried by the wind. Standard pulsar magnetosphere theory implies σ ≫ 1 just outside the light cylinder, while ideal-MHD modelling of the nebular flow requires σ ≲ 1 at the upstream side of the wind termination shock in order for the shock to decelerate the flow to the slow expansion speeds observed in objects such as the Crab Nebula.

Within the framework of three-dimensional ideal relativistic MHD (allowing kink and other current-driven instabilities, and the associated turbulent reconnection/dissipation of magnetic energy in the striped wind zone and inside the nebula), determine:

(a) the mechanism and quantitative efficiency by which σ is reduced (or its energy redistributed into particle kinetic energy and thermal/non-thermal pressure) between the light cylinder and the termination shock, starting from initial wind magnetizations σ ≫ 1;

(b) whether such 3D high-σ MHD evolution self-consistently yields a volume-averaged nebular magnetic field of order ∼ 200 μG (the value inferred for the Crab Nebula from multiwavelength observations) at the present evolutionary stage; and

(c) whether the resulting synthetic non-thermal (synchrotron and inverse-Compton) emission spectrum and morphology, computed from the simulated particle distribution and magnetic field, match the observed broadband emission of the Crab Nebula across radio, optical, X-ray, and γ-ray bands.
artifact.category_tag: Relativistic MHD of pulsar wind nebulae
artifact.status_search_result: Three-dimensional relativistic MHD simulations (Porth, Komissarov & Keppens 2013/2014) demonstrated that current-driven kink instabilities randomize the toroidal magnetic field and trigger magnetic dissipation inside the nebula, allowing initially Poynting-dominated winds (up to σ ≈ 3) to be reconciled with the observed termination-shock radius and slow expansion of the Crab Nebula — partially resolving the σ problem dynamically. However, quantitative reproduction of the volume-averaged nebular magnetic field (~200 μG) and of the broadband non-thermal emission across all bands from first-principles 3D high-σ MHD remains incomplete, with subsequent works (e.g., on confinement and global particle-acceleration models) still addressing these issues.

status_evidence.title: Solution to the sigma problem of pulsar wind nebulae (Porth, Komissarov & Keppens 2013)
status_evidence.snippet: 3D relativistic MHD simulations show kink instability randomizes the toroidal field and drives magnetic dissipation, reconciling Poynting-dominated pulsar winds with observed nebula dynamics.
status_evidence.claim: Dynamical σ problem partially resolved by 3D MHD via kink-driven dissipation.

status_evidence.title: Three-dimensional MHD simulations of the Crab nebula (MNRAS 438, 278)
status_evidence.snippet: Simulations with σ up to 3 reproduce the termination-shock size and produce a particle-dominated, roughly uniform total pressure inside the nebula.
status_evidence.claim: 3D high-σ MHD reproduces key dynamical features of the Crab Nebula.

status_evidence.title: Confinement of the Crab Nebula with tangled magnetic field by its SNR (1805.08325)
status_evidence.snippet: Subsequent work continues to investigate the magnetic-field structure and confinement of the Crab Nebula.
status_evidence.claim: Quantitative match of nebular B-field and broadband emission still under active study.

status_evidence.title: A global model of particle acceleration at pulsar wind termination shocks (A&A 2020)
status_evidence.snippet: Recent global modelling addresses non-thermal emission from termination-shock acceleration.
status_evidence.claim: Reproducing full broadband non-thermal emission self-consistently remains an open modelling problem.
